headings.title: Introduction to Nutrition Counselling in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Nutrition counselling is a fundamental component of primary health care delivery across Nigeria. It bridges the gap between clinical diagnoses and community-level wellbeing by helping patients make informed food choices. Nurses often serve as the primary educators, translating complex dietary science into practical, everyday habits. Effective counselling prevents malnutrition, manages chronic conditions like hypertension and diabetes, and supports optimal maternal and child health outcomes. Rather than simply handing out pamphlets, the process involves a collaborative dialogue between the healthcare provider and the client.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Dietary History Taking
headings.content:
A thorough nutritional assessment forms the foundation of any effective dietary intervention. Nurses must gather baseline data before recommending changes.

- **Anthropometric measurements**: Tracking height, weight, mid-upper arm circumference, and body mass index to gauge physical status.
- **Clinical examination**: Inspecting skin, hair, eyes, and nails for physical signs of nutrient deficiencies.
- **Dietary history**: Documenting a typical 24-hour food recall or a food frequency questionnaire to understand usual intake.
- **Biochemical data**: Reviewing laboratory results such as packed cell volume or serum protein levels when available.

headings.title: Identifying Vulnerable Groups and Dietary Deficiencies
headings.content: Certain populations face a higher risk of malnutrition due to physiological demands, socioeconomic factors, or cultural practices. Pregnant and lactating women, infants, young children, and the elderly require vigilant monitoring. Common deficiencies in the region include protein-energy malnutrition, iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin A deficiency, and iodine disorders. Recognizing early clinical signs—such as pale conjunctiva, Bitot's spots, or delayed growth milestones—enables prompt intervention and prevents long-term developmental damage.

headings.title: Communication Techniques and Behaviour Change
headings.content: Telling a patient what to eat rarely works without effective communication. Active listening builds trust and uncovers hidden barriers to healthy eating. Using open-ended questions encourages clients to share their real challenges rather than giving the answers they think the nurse wants to hear. Motivational interviewing helps resolve ambivalence about changing deeply ingrained dietary habits. The focus remains on empowering the client to take charge of their own health decisions.

headings.title: Developing Culturally Acceptable Meal Plans
headings.content: A meal plan is useless if it ignores local food availability, household income, and cultural food preferences. When counseling a patient in Nigeria, nurses must recommend readily available local staples like millet, sorghum, yam, cassava, beans, and leafy green vegetables. Advice should maximize the nutritional value of traditional dishes rather than introducing expensive, foreign ingredients. Involving family members who prepare the meals ensures that recommendations are realistic and sustainable at home.

headings.title: Addressing Barriers and Follow-Up Care
headings.content: Economic hardship, limited food storage, and persistent cultural myths often hinder proper nutrition. Nurses must identify these hurdles early and brainstorm realistic workarounds with the client. Follow-up visits allow the healthcare team to evaluate progress, reinforce positive changes, and adjust meal plans when circumstances shift. Continuous support transforms temporary dietary fixes into lifelong healthy behaviors.
